newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY SIGNS CONTESTED TV CHANNEL FRANCHISES.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY SIGNS CONTESTED TV CHANNEL FRANCHISES.

text.p: Hungary on Wednesday signed 10-year concessions for two national commercial TV channels with Luxembourg-based CLT's Magyar RTL and Swedish-Hungarian consortium MTM-SBS.
The CLT-led consortium, Magyar RTL, includes Raiffeisen Unicbank, British group Pearson , publisher of the Financial Times, and Hungarian telecommunications company Matav.
MTM-SBS is a consortium of the Hungarian-registered company MTM Kommunikacios, TeleMunchen and the majority U.S.-owned company Scandinavian Broadcasting System.
Magyar RTL offered nine billion forints ($47.6 million) for the channel it won, while MTM-SBS offered the set minimum of eight billion forints for the other commercial channel.
Irisz TV, a consortium led by Central European Media Enterprises of the U.S., offered 12.5 billion and 12 billion forints, respectively, for the two channels but failed in both bids.
It is challenging the decision and has asked a court to forbid signing of the concession contracts.
It said the ORTT, the Hungarian radio and television body which awarded the concessions, had breached regulations when assessing the bids and violated the tender procedures.
On Wednesday it announced it had a public document showing that one of the winning tenders was illegal.

After the signing ORTT Chairman Mihaly Revesz said he had no comment on the statement. The case would be settled in court. "I haven't seen (the statement) and I don't have any comment, especially as this is an ongoing legal process."

The eight-member ORTT board chose the winning bidders after two rounds of discussion, saying one important factor was the future diversity of Hungary's media scene and that the verdict was unanimous but for one abstention.
The 10-year franchises can be extended by another five years without the need for a second tender. The two TV channels will have to start broadcasting on October 7 at the latest.

Seven years of political wrangling have left Hungary's media privatisation trailing behind that in other former communist countries such as Poland and the Czech Republic, which already have commercial national television stations. ($ = 189.1 Hungarian Forints)
